opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I've been thinking about a lot. It's actually where the name "Cambrian" in some of our recent work comes from.

There's a hypothesis I find very inspiring, from the zoologist Andrew Parker, called the "light switch" theory. Around 540 million years ago, in a geologically very short window, we see this sudden explosion in the diversity of animal life. Almost all the major body plans we know today appear in the fossil record. One explanation for why it happened so fast is that this is roughly when the first true eyes evolved.

Before eyes, organisms could only sense their environment in a very local, passive way, through touch, chemical gradients, maybe crude light sensitivity. Once you can actually *see*, everything changes. Predators can hunt actively from a distance. Prey must evolve defenses: armor, shells, camouflage, speed. It becomes an arms race, and that pressure drives enormous diversification in body forms, behaviors and nervous systems.

So to me, the deeper point is that vision isn't just one sense among many. It's the interface through which an organism builds a model of the world and acts in it. Intelligence, in a biological sense, co-evolved with perception. You need to perceive the world before you can reason about it, plan in it, or survive in it.

That's why I think it matters for AI right now. Much of the recent progress has come from language models, and language is incredibly powerful, but it's a very compressed, human-made abstraction of the world. Animals developed rich, grounded intelligence long before any language existed, and vision was central to that. If we want systems that really understand the physical world, that have something like spatial intelligence or a world model, I don't think we can treat vision as a plug-in to a language model. It probably needs to be a foundation.

So when I look at the Cambrian explosion, I see a kind of analogy, maybe also a hope: once machines can truly see, not just label images but perceive and understand space, time and physical dynamics, we might see a similar explosion in what AI systems can do.

r001.rationale: The response describes the evolution of eyes enabling distant predation, prompting prey defenses and an arms race that drove diversification.

r002.rationale: It connects the eyes-driven predator–prey arms race to the rapid diversification associated with the Cambrian explosion.

fable-5.1.text:
The Cambrian explosion is actually where we got the name for our project, Cambrian-1, so I've thought about this quite a bit. Roughly 540 million years ago, you see this sudden burst in the diversity of animal life, and there's a hypothesis, Andrew Parker's "light switch" theory, that the evolution of eyes was a key trigger. Once organisms could sense light and form images, the whole dynamic between predator and prey changed. You could see something coming and run; you could spot food and chase it. That created enormous selective pressure for bodies that move, for shells, for camouflage, and for nervous systems that can process all of that incoming information and turn it into action.

What I take from that is that vision didn't evolve as a passive recording device. It co-evolved with behavior and with the brain. Perception existed because it was useful for doing something in the world. I think that's the right lens for thinking about AI today. A lot of the field treats vision as a sort of add-on to language models, where you bolt on an encoder, feed in some image tokens, and call it multimodal. But if we take the biological analogy seriously, vision should be foundational, and it should be grounded in interaction, in sensorimotor experience, not just in captions scraped from the web.

So when I look at the current moment, I see something similar to that pre-Cambrian period. We have very capable language systems, but they're a bit like organisms without eyes. Once we figure out how to give these systems a real sense of the physical world, how to let them learn representations from the environment itself rather than from text about the environment, I think we'll see a comparable diversification in what these systems can do. That's the bet we're making with Cambrian: the study of vision isn't a sub-problem of language, it's a parallel path toward intelligence, and maybe the more fundamental one.

r001.rationale: The response says a leading theory treats the evolution of eyes as a key trigger and describes changed predator–prey dynamics, but it does not identify an arms race in visual ability among species.

r002.rationale: The response presents vision as a possible trigger for the Cambrian explosion, but does not say that an arms race in visual ability drove the diversification of species.

astra-6.text:
I think vision is a fascinating way to think about the Cambrian explosion, because it changes how an organism can interact with the world. Instead of waiting until something touches you, you can detect something at a distance—a predator, prey, or an obstacle—and act before contact happens.

There’s a hypothesis that the evolution of eyes helped drive an evolutionary arms race. Once some animals could see and hunt more effectively, others faced pressure to develop better defenses, camouflage, or movement. Those changes, in turn, made better perception more valuable. You can imagine this feedback loop contributing to the diversification of animals.

But I would be careful about saying vision caused the Cambrian explosion. It’s a hypothesis about one important factor in a much more complicated process.

What I find especially interesting, from an AI perspective, is that vision becomes useful through action. You have to interpret what you see, decide what matters, and respond. So the connection isn’t simply that eyes produce more information; it’s that perception creates new possibilities for behavior, and new demands on intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response says the evolution of eyes may have started an evolutionary arms race: seeing and hunting improved, prompting other animals to develop better defenses, camouflage, or movement.

r002.rationale: It says this feedback loop may have contributed to animal diversification and frames vision as one important factor in the Cambrian explosion, while cautioning against treating it as the sole cause.

sol-6.1.text:
I think vision offers a fascinating way to think about the Cambrian explosion. The idea is that once organisms could see, they gained a much richer way to sense their environment: they could detect prey, recognize predators, and act at a distance. That could create an evolutionary arms race—better perception puts pressure on other organisms to develop better camouflage, faster movement, or more effective defenses.

I wouldn’t say vision alone explains the Cambrian explosion. But the interesting hypothesis is that improvements in perception can change the whole ecosystem. Seeing becomes useful only when you can interpret what you see and take action, so perception, intelligence, and behavior start evolving together.

That connection is also what makes vision so interesting to me as an AI researcher. It’s more than assigning a label to an image. It’s a way of understanding the world that enables an agent to interact with it.

r001.rationale: The response describes vision prompting an arms race in camouflage, speed, and defenses, but does not identify an arms race in visual ability among species or attribute that claim to a leading theory.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that an arms race in visual ability drove the Cambrian explosion of species; it describes broader ecological effects and says vision alone does not explain the explosion.
